prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

My desk is cleared of the litter of ages; Before me glitter the fair white pages; My fountain pen is clean and filled, And the noise of the office has long been stilled. Roget’s Thesaurus is at my hand, And I’m ready to do some work that’s grand, Dignified, eminent, great, momentous, Memorable, worthy of note, portentous, Beautiful, paramount, vital, prime, Stirring, eventful, august, sublime. For this is the way, I have read and heard, That authors look for the fitting word. All of the proud ingredients mine To build, like Marlowe, the mighty line. But never a line from my new-filled pen That couldn’t be done by a child of ten. Oh, how did Shelley and how did Keats Weave magic words on the fair white sheets Under conditions that, were they mine, I couldn’t bear? And I’d just resign. Yet Milton wrote passable literature Under conditions I couldn’t endure. Coleridge and Chatterton did their stuff Over a road that I’d christen rough. Wordsworth and—soft!—could it be that they Waited until they had something to say?

outputs.L1:
Here are two ways to polish the text, depending on the format you prefer:

### Option 1: Professional Eloquent Prose (Ideal for essays, speeches, or formal writing)

My workspace has finally been cleared of the accumulated clutter of the past. Before me lie pristine, blank pages, while my fountain pen stands clean, refilled, and ready. The clamor of the office has long since faded into silence. With Roget’s Thesaurus at arm’s reach, I am prepared to undertake a monumental labor—to craft a work that is noble, eminent, momentous, and sublime. This, I have gathered, is the timeless process by which great authors pursue the precise word, assembling every essential element to forge a mighty line in the tradition of Marlowe. 

Yet, despite this immaculate preparation, the prose flowing from my pen remains utterly pedestrian—no more sophisticated than the work of a young child. I am left to wonder how literary icons like Shelley and Keats wove such enduring magic under conditions so intolerable that I would have surrendered instantly. Milton produced classic literature amidst adversity I could never endure, just as Coleridge and Chatterton navigated paths far rougher than any I have known. Then the true realization strikes: perhaps Wordsworth and the great masters succeeded not because of their ideal environment, but because they simply waited until they had something meaningful to say.

---

### Option 2: Elevated Poetic Verse (Maintaining the rhyming format with enhanced diction)

My workspace is purged of the clutter of time;  
Before me lie pages pristine and sublime.  
My fountain pen rests now replenished and clear,  
While the din of the office yields silence sincere.  
With Roget’s Thesaurus positioned near,  
I stand prepared for a grand career—  
To craft a work stately, transcendent, profound,  
Momentous, distinguished, where wonders abound,  
August, evocative, vital, sublime,  
Resonant across the expanse of time.  

For thus, I am told, do the masters prepare  
To capture the phrase of perfection and care,  
Assembling the elements, noble and fine,  
To forge, like great Marlowe, a glorious line.  

Yet alas, from the nib of this newly filled pen  
Flows nothing surpassing a child of ten.  
How did Shelley and Keats weave such wondrous prose  
Amid hardship and trial that I’d never brave?  
Milton crafted his masterpieces rare  
Through burdens I couldn’t endure or bear.  
And Coleridge and Chatterton triumphed through strife,  
Navigating a bitter and arduous life.  
While Wordsworth... but soft! Could the truth be conveyed?  
Did they simply refrain till they had something to say?

***

Years of accumulated clutter have finally been swept off my workspace, leaving bright, unused paper lying ready before me. My pen has been thoroughly washed and replenished with fresh ink, and all workplace commotion has completely faded away. Resting nearby is a volume of synonyms, putting me in the perfect position to produce a magnificent creation—something regal, distinguished, monumental, breathtaking, crucial, and deeply moving. From what I’ve gathered through stories and studies, this preparation is how legendary writers discover the exact vocabulary they need. I have gathered every single component required to construct majestic, impactful verse in the style of Christopher Marlowe.

However, the words flowing from my freshly loaded pen are so basic that a ten-year-old child could have composed them. I cannot comprehend how poets like Shelley and Keats managed to craft enchanting literature on blank sheets while facing miserable environments—hardships so intense that I would have quit instantly. Likewise, Milton created respectable works under circumstances I find intolerable, while Coleridge and Chatterton achieved greatness along extremely difficult journeys. But as I consider Wordsworth, a sudden thought strikes me: could it be that these great literary figures simply held back on putting pen to paper until they actually had a meaningful idea to convey?
outputs.L3:
I set the stage for creation with meticulous care. The room was bathed in total silence, blissfully insulated from the chaotic hum of the outside world. My desk was a model of pristine organization: smooth, heavy-gauge paper aligned precisely beside a favorite fountain pen, bathed in the soft glow of a desk lamp. I had curated the ultimate workspace, convinced that in such a sacred, orderly sanctuary, a literary masterpiece would naturally be born.

There is a seductive delusion in the writing world that the right environment guarantees greatness. As I sat down, I was buoyed by the belief that proper preparation and high-quality tools were the true precursors to artistic achievement. I fully expected to craft noble, unforgettable poetry—words that would echo with profound emotion and timeless beauty. With my physical surroundings so perfectly aligned, it seemed impossible for the writing to be anything less than extraordinary.

Yet, as pen finally met paper, the grand illusion shattered. Despite the flawless working conditions, the well of inspiration proved entirely dry. What emerged was not sweeping, majestic verse, but trite, simplistic lines—monotonous rhymes and elementary thoughts that even a child could have written without effort. The pristine page was now marred by mediocrity, and the quiet of the room, once so comforting, began to mock the barrenness of my mind.

In my disappointment, my thoughts turned to the giants of literary history. I marveled at how John Keats could craft his heartbreaking, sublime odes while battling poverty and a fatal illness, or how Percy Bysshe Shelley produced such fiery, transcendent poetry amid political turmoil and personal exile. I thought of John Milton, who, entirely blind and living through the aftermath of a civil war, dictated the monumental cosmos of *Paradise Lost*. None of these masters possessed ergonomic chairs, climate-controlled studies, or pristine silence. They wrote in severe, uncomfortable, and often tragic conditions, yet managed to capture the sublime.

It was then that I arrived at a humbling realization: great literature is not summoned by an organized desk or a expensive pen, but by an inner urgency. The true secret of the legendary authors was not their setup, but their substance. They succeeded because they waited—or were forced by life—until they possessed a fiery conviction, a deep truth, or an overwhelming emotion that demanded to be shared. The ultimate lesson of my quiet evening was simple: art does not begin when the workspace is ready, but when the writer finally has something meaningful to say.
outputs.L4:
I convinced myself that the birth of a literary masterpiece required a sanctuary of absolute perfection. For weeks, I focused my energies not on the act of writing, but on constructing the ultimate environment for genius to flourish. I selected a quiet corner of the house, far removed from the ambient noise of the street. Upon a polished wooden desk, I laid out my sacred tools: a stack of pristine, cream-colored paper, a heavy fountain pen freshly filled with deep indigo ink, and a leather-bound thesaurus sitting ready like a trusted advisor. Everything was immaculately arranged, designed to coax the dormant muse into the light.

When the moment finally arrived, I sat down, took a deep breath, and rested the nib of the pen against the unblemished page. I waited for the profound, sweeping prose to flow effortlessly from my mind. Yet, as the ink began to dry, the words staring back at me were startlingly mediocre. Instead of timeless insight, I produced simple, trite observations and wooden, childish phrasing. My grand ideas, once put to paper, read like the naive scribblings of an elementary school assignment. Despite the flawless quiet and the exquisite instruments, the magic simply wasn’t there.

Staring at the disappointing pages, a humbling realization began to dawn on me. I looked at my luxurious surroundings and thought of the legendary authors whose work had shaped the world. They had not required soundproof rooms, hand-milled paper, or perfectly balanced pens to capture the human experience. Dostoyevsky wrote under the crushing weight of debt and fear; Emily Dickinson penned transcendent verse on scraps of used envelopes; trench poets wrote enduring lines amid the mud and horror of war. 

Their masterpieces were forged not in comfort, but in the crucible of real life. They succeeded not because they possessed optimal surroundings, but because they possessed genuine, urgent insights to express—truths born of suffering, observation, and profound feeling. I had mistakenly believed that the craft lived in the tools, forgetting that a fountain pen is merely a vessel. Without a vital story to tell, even the quietest room and the finest paper will yield nothing more than quiet, empty words.
outputs.L5:
**Before** the mid-nineteenth century, writers seeking the perfect word to express a nuanced thought were largely left to their own memory. Dictionaries of the era were exceptional at defining words you already knew, but they offered little help if a concept was dancing just out of reach at the edge of your mind. 

Enter Peter Mark **Roget**, a British physician, scientist, **and** scholar. Throughout his life, Roget had a obsessive passion for classifying things. To cope with personal tragedy and keep his mind active, he compiled vast lists of words, arranging them not alphabetically, but by their underlying meanings and relationships. 

When he finally published his *Thesaurus of English Words and Phrases* in 1852, it revolutionized the literary world. **Before** this monumental release, there was no systematic bridge connecting a vague idea **and** its precise verbal expression. **Roget** categorized the English language into six primary classes—ranging from abstract relations to moral powers—creating an intellectual map of human thought.

Today, the name **Roget** is synonymous with the thesaurus itself. His painstaking effort transformed how we navigate language, ensuring that writers would always have a tool to connect their innermost thoughts **and** the exact words needed to bring them to life.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lighthearted, rhyming poem about an aspiring writer who has a perfectly prepared desk and a thesaurus, but suffers from writer's block and realizes classic poets like Keats and Milton actually had something meaningful to say.
counterfactuals.output:
My ergonomic chair is set, my posture is pristine,
A cozy glow of readiness reflects upon the screen.
My mug of craft French-roast is hot, my succulent is green,
I’m poised to write the greatest prose the world has ever seen!

My fountain pen is freshly inked, my desk is cleared of clutter,
I’ve silenced every app to stop my mind from taking flutter.
And resting right beside my hand, a total work of art:
A heavy, bound Thesaurus, ready to ignite my heart.

I open up its sacred pages, hunting for a phrase,
To turn my humble, modest thoughts into a purple haze.
Why settle for a word like "sad" when *dismal* sounds so grand?
I’ll weave grandiloquent delights across this digital land!

Yet as I sit expectantly into the blinding white,
The cursor blinks mockingly into the silent night.
An hour passes, cold and still; my coffee’s turned to mud,
My brain is like a dried-up sponge, devoid of creative blood.

I rearrange my colored pens! I wipe my laptop screen!
I check the font size once again—is twelve a bit too lean?
I tweak the desk lamp’s warm display, I dust the wooden shelf...
I've done *everything* to write, except for write itself.

In desperation for a spark, I pull down ancient books,
To see how legendary bards accrued their famous looks.
I flipped through Keats's famous odes, expecting shiny style—
Just clever words to charm the crowd and make the critics smile.

Instead, I found a soaring heart—with beauty, grief, and truth!
A depth of real emotion that survived his fleeting youth.
I skimmed through Milton’s epic lines of darkness and of light,
And realized the man had *thoughts* that burned within his sight.

They didn't just hoard synonyms to pad a pretty verse;
They actually had *things to say* about the universe!
They felt the weight of love and loss, of cosmos, fate, and soul,
While I was hoping *syzygy* would make my sentence whole.

So here I sit with pastel pens and lo-fi beats on loop,
A master of aesthetics, feeling like a nincompoop.
Turns out a perfectly curated desk won't grant a grand design—
I need to get a life to write, and leave big words behind!
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a funny poem about writer's block.
counterfactuals.output:
The blinking cursor sits and sneers
Upon a screen of blinding white.
It mocks my hopes, it feeds my fears—
I’ve typed three words since eight tonight.

Those three words were: *“Chapter One: The…”*
Which I erased, then typed again.
My mind has gone entirely numb,
Outsmarted by a digital pen.

So I distract my lazy brain
With tasks I usually despise.
I scrubbed the sink, cleared out the drain,
And sorted all my socks by size.

I checked the fridge eleven times,
Expecting gourmet treats to grow.
I researched medieval crimes,
And learned how fast a sloth can go.

I’m six cups deep in hot caffeine,
My left leg twitches like a clock.
My eyelid vibrates, tense and mean—
Is this a stroke, or Writer’s Block?

My grand idea has up and fled,
My muse has gone to Trinidad.
My epic novel’s officially dead...
Wait. 
Writing about this isn't bad! 

I’ve filled a page! I’ve cracked the spell!
My sudden genius makes me smile!
Now I can rest and brag as well...
(After I nap a little while).
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: I'm sitting at my clean desk with a filled fountain pen and Roget's Thesaurus, ready to write a masterpiece, but my brain is completely empty. Write a witty comic verse capturing this exact struggle and comparing my situation to literary legends like Shelley, Keats, and Wordsworth.
counterfactuals.output:
The blotter is spotless, the desk is pristine,
My fountain pen filled with the deepest marine;
Old Roget sits open, a lexicon feast,
Ready to unleash a poetic great beast.
I am primed for a masterpiece, noble and grand,
With the tool of a genius gripped tight in my hand!

Yet deep in my skull, where the magic should brew,
There isn’t a concept, a glimmer, a clue.
My brain is a desert, a vacuum, a void,
With all of my brilliant ambitions destroyed.

Will Wordsworth could gaze at a single damp weed
And churn out an epic with staggering speed;
Ten thousand bright daffodils danced in the breeze,
And he tossed off a classic with elegant ease.
I’m staring at plaster, expecting a spark,
But my cranium echoes like caves in the dark.

Young Keats heard a bird in a dim-dappled glade
And *poof!* an immortal, magnificent Ode!
He swooned at an urn with a tear in his eye,
And found cosmic truth in a autumn-tinged sky.
I swoon at my desk, but it’s purely from strain,
As I try to wring art from a desiccated brain.

And Shelley! Wild Shelley commanded the Wind!
He sang to a Skylark, unhinged and unpinned,
With fiery passions that thundered and roared
As his glorious verses magnificently soared.
My muse hasn't soared; she has taken a nap,
Leaving me with a full pen and nothing to map.

I consult Mr. Roget for *empty* and *numb*,
Finding *vacuous*, *hollow*, *insipid*, and *dumb*.
The paper gleams white, and the nib remains wet...
It’s the greatest blank page that I’ve written as yet!
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a humorous light verse about the futility of over-preparing your workspace, including a line where the narrator literally reads off a list of synonyms from a thesaurus.
counterfactuals.output:
I sat down to work at the start of the day,
Determined to drive all distractions away.
I straightened my notepad, aligned every pen,
Then dusted the lamp-base, and dusted again.

I adjusted my chair to a ninety-degree bend,
Untangled the cords from beginning to end.
I fetched a cold water, I brewed a hot tea,
And aligned my dual monitors ergonomically.

To make sure my prose would be punchy and bright,
I grabbed a thesaurus to get the tone right.
I looked up *Delay*, and to clear out my head,
I pointed my finger and literally read:

*“Postpone, dither, temporize, linger, defer,
Shelve, tarry, procrastinate, loiter, demur.”*

My workspace was pristine, a glorious sight,
Harmonious, balanced, and lit just right.
Not a paperclip strayed! Not a speck of dust stayed!
...And I’d wasted eight hours getting ready to trade.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you generate a retro-style humorous poem about writer's block that references famous historical poets, uses AABB rhyming couplets, and ends with a punchline about having nothing to say?
counterfactuals.output:
I dip my fountain pen in India ink,
And sit beside the windowpane to think.
My trusty Underwood sits on the stand,
With blank paper waiting for my hand.

Great Shakespeare churned out plays with easy grace,
While Byron wrote of love at frantic pace.
Young Edgar Allan Poe found gothic woes,
In raven wings to paint his haunting prose.

Will Wordsworth saw a yellow daffodil,
And poetry came pouring from his quill.
And Emily, sequestered from the crowd,
Wrote brilliant verse without a sound aloud.

Yet here I sit, a miserable wretch,
Without a single clever line to sketch.
I toss another paper in the bin,
And wonder where on earth I should begin.

I curse the silent, ticking parlor clock,
For bringing on this dreadful writer's block!
My tragic plight is clear as sunny day:
I simply haven't got a thing to say!
